item.title: Datacentres to create 70% more carbon emissions by 2030, IEA report warns
item.description:
Global energy watchdog forecasts huge rise as US and China turn to fossil fuels to power AI growth agendas

The world’s datacentres will create 70% more carbon emissions within the next four years as the US and China turn to fossil fuels to power their AI growth agendas, according to the world’s energy watchdog.

The International Energy Agency (IEA) warned that datacentres will consume twice as much electricity by 2030 compared with today, with the global expansion of artificial intelligence accounting for three-quarters of this growth.

item.title: Andy Burnham is in danger of over-selling his big Brussels summit. What happens if he under-delivers? | Joël Reland
item.description:
In laying a trap for himself, the PM could derail his longer-term ambition of revisiting Brexit

This week’s UK-EU summit may, one day, be seen as the start of the UK’s long march back towards the EU. Andy Burnham’s much-anticipated first meeting with EU chiefs in Brussels on Friday will be used to unveil a suite of detailed agreements to improve trade and economic cooperation, before the Prime Minister kickstarts his longer term “national conversation” about a much closer form of political and economic relationship with the EU. This, as Burnham signalled in a speech on Monday night, could well culminate in Labour’s next election manifesto abandoning the party’s famous red lines, and proposing an application for EU membership.

For pro-Europeans, this must read like a fever dream. Just four months ago, when Burnham took office, such a bold offer on Europe from the Labour party seemed implausible. But while Burnham has certainly reinvigorated the Brexit debate, he will have to move carefully to avoid storing up trouble for himself down the road. There is a risk that Burnham will come to be seen as someone who over-promises and under-delivers on Europe – and, in doing so, halts the growing momentum around revisiting the troublesome Brexit question.

Joël Reland is senior researcher at the UK in a Changing Europe thinktank

item.title: Crimea bridge has been attacked again, says Russian-installed governor
item.description:
Assessment of damage is underway, days after two attacks that destroyed road section of key bridge across Kerch strait linking annexed peninsula to Russia

A key bridge connecting annexed Crimea to Russia has been attacked again, a Russian-appointed regional governor has said, two days after Ukrainian strikes caused serious damage to it.

“Following a new attack on the Crimean Bridge, traffic has been temporarily halted. All relevant services are on site and at work. An assessment of the damage is under way,” Sergei Aksyonov, the Kremlin-appointed governor of Crimea, wrote on Telegram.
